Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations

Written and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A kernel has two covector components. Either component may vanish although the pair is singular. Those zero components determine whether a kernel can act on a distribution, and even a zero intermediate covector can carry a singularity through a composition. We develop products, integration and kernel action with these cases included, and prove the convergence statement that makes extension from smooth inputs unique.

Pairings are complex-linear. Our Fourier transform is , with inverse factor . Open sets lie in Euclidean spaces. A closed conic subset of a nonzero cotangent space is closed relative to that space.

The exact earlier proofs used here are Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B3 and Theorem 1.1, for locality, parameter pairings, tensor products, their supports and limits, and convolution; Order, positivity and distributional limits, Theorem 5.1, for common finite-order bounds of weakly convergent sequences; Derivative growth and finite-order localization, Lemmas 1 and 5 and Theorem 4, for fixed index shifts, bounded compact distributions and controlled cutoffs; and Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorems 3–7, for compact conic localization, class comparisons, singular support and multiplication by a function.

Analytic pullback and cotangent directions, Theorems 2, 4 and 6, proves the all-class pullback inclusion and exact diffeomorphism and submersion formulas. Its supplied smooth pullback reading, Sections 18.1–18.5, gives the complete ordinary construction and Fourier estimates. We use that construction; below we prove the additional convergence properties. Fourier inversion, Gaussian normalization and convolution identities are proved in the Schwartz prerequisite, F1–F5. Compact cutoffs and integration are supplied in the metric, Sections 13.1–13.10, and integration, Sections 15–16, prerequisites.

Convolution as a kernel consequence

Corollary 7 (convolution directions). If and , then

The ordinary version and the conic continuity of the corresponding kernel action hold as well. Smooth compact inputs give smooth outputs, continuously for the usual fixed-support smooth convergence.

Proof. Set , the pullback by the analytic submersion . Exact submersion covariance gives . Both endpoint-axis sets (15) are empty. Thus every compact satisfies the normal exclusion, and the relation term in (17) is exactly (24). For smooth compact , measure substitution in the distributional pairing identifies the action with . For general compact , conic smooth approximation, Theorem 5, and B3 and Theorem 1.1 of the convolution lesson pass this identity to the limit. This identifies the construction with the earlier convolution, including its normalization. The ordinary convergence assertion follows from Theorem 5 with empty input normal set. When the input cone is empty, its approximating transforms have uniform rapid decrease in all directions. The resulting output has empty ordinary wavefront; moreover (7) in all directions implies local convergence of every derivative by Fourier inversion, using an integrable inverse power larger than the derivative order plus dimension. This proves the stated smooth continuity.

If a factor space has dimension zero, its open set is empty or a point. Distributions on a point are scalars, their nonzero cotangent spaces are empty, tensoring is scalar multiplication and integration is the identity or multiplication by the scalar. The definitions and proofs above reduce to these statements. The formulas also hold for empty supports and the zero distribution.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 — a zero endpoint is indispensable. Compute the wavefront of on for every , and explain why the product of the two nonzero wavefront sets is insufficient in (2).

Solution. The one-dimensional point mass has every nonzero covector over zero, as proved in U074 after Theorem 7. Exact projection covariance in U083 therefore gives . The second factor has empty wavefront, so the product of the two nonzero wavefront sets is empty. Its support-times-zero term supplies every direction in this example. The ordinary answer is the same.

Exercise 2 — crossing two point-mass walls. On , form the product of and . Identify both the distribution and its wavefront.

Solution. Their wavefront covectors are respectively on , and on . No nonzero opposite pair exists, so the product is defined. Take compact mollifiers , in the normal variables. They converge conically by the proof of Lemma 3 and the exact projection formula. Their smooth product pairs with a test as its double average around , tending to the test's value there. Product continuity gives . Every cutoff equal to one near the origin leaves its Fourier transform equal to one. Thus every nonzero covector there is in the ordinary wavefront, hence in every ; away from the origin it vanishes. Formula (12) includes the axial directions through its zero terms and all other directions through addition of the two nonzero normal components.

Exercise 3 — a divergent regularization of a square. Explain the failure of (11) for on the line. For the normalized Gaussian , determine the leading size of when .

Solution. Both signs are in the wavefront of , giving an opposite pair. Substituting gives

Dominated convergence applies after extracting the prefactor, since is bounded and the Gaussian integrable. Thus these squares have no distributional limit. This disproves existence of this particular unrenormalized approximation; failure of a sufficient wavefront condition is not a general theorem forbidding every separately specified product.

Exercise 5 — a composition carried by zero. Let , and , where is smooth, compactly supported and . Prove that restricting the matched middle covector to be nonzero gives a false composition bound, even if both outer-axis terms in (22) are kept.

Solution. The support of is compact, hence proper over . The input-normal set of is empty by Exercise 1, so (20) holds. Direct action gives and , hence . At any point where , the ordinary wavefront of includes for every in primed notation: locally multiplication by the smooth nonvanishing and its inverse preserves the wavefront of . These directions also belong to every . Thus and match at middle covector zero, yielding outer pairs with both components nonzero. If zero were forbidden in the matching, the main composition term would be empty. The two terms (22) supply only outer axes and miss all such pairs. The proposed narrower bound is therefore false.

Exercise 7 — the condition at infinity. On three copies of the line, take . All their wavefronts are empty. Explain why Theorem 6 nevertheless cannot be applied.

Solution. The support of is , whose inverse image of a nonempty compact set in contains every ; its projection is not proper. For with , is the constant function one. Exercise 8 — pairwise tests do not check a triple. In a two-dimensional cotangent fiber take the three positive rays generated by , and . Test the pairwise and joint conditions used in Theorem 4.

Solution. No two rays contain nonzero opposite vectors: the first two have different coordinate axes, and the third has two strictly negative coordinates. Hence all pairwise no-opposition tests pass. But is a sum with all three terms nonzero. Condition (13) fails. The partial sum cone of the first two contains , opposite to the third ray, so the second multiplication cannot be justified by that theorem's hypotheses. This is a counterexample to an implication between cone conditions, not an assertion that every particular triple of distributions with these cone bounds has an undefined product.
